title: Conditions for Great Teams
text:
J. Richard Hackman of Harvard spent decades studying teams in their natural habitats: airline cockpit crews, symphony orchestras, hospital teams, factory groups and many others. Again and again he saw managers try to fix a struggling team by coaching it in the moment or sending it on a team-building retreat, with little lasting effect.

In his 2002 book Leading Teams, Hackman argued that a team's success depends mostly on conditions set up before and around the work. He named five. It must be a real team, with clear membership, a shared task and enough stability to learn to work together. It needs a compelling direction, a purpose that is clear, challenging and important. It needs an enabling structure: a well designed task, the right size and mix of people, and clear norms of conduct. It needs a supportive organizational context that provides information, training and rewards for the team as a whole. And it benefits from expert coaching at the right moments, such as the start, the midpoint and the end of a piece of work.

Hackman found that when these conditions were in place, teams tended to manage themselves well. When they were missing, even talented members and skilled leaders struggled.
lesson: Before trying to fix a team's chemistry, check its setup. Clear membership, a purpose worth caring about and a well designed task do more than any pep talk.
source: Hackman, J. R. (2002). Leading Teams: Setting the Stage for Great Performances. Harvard Business School Press.
